title: Keeping water liquid in winter
summary: How to keep a household's water from freezing when the house is cold: a day's supply in the warm room, part-filled jugs, a cooler used as a warm box, and flasks and bottles kept in the sleeping bag. Frozen jugs split, a germ filter that froze wet may let germs through and can't be reliably checked, and cold water needs double the bleach and a longer wait.

materials.item: Clean, food-grade plastic jugs and bottles with caps
materials.qty: a day's water per person, about 4 L

materials.item: Towels, blankets, cardboard or crumpled paper to pack round bottles
Rubber hot-water bottle in a cover

steps.text: Pick the warm room and keep at least a day's water there in capped containers: about 4 L per person (Get Prepared kits).
Fill any container that may freeze only part-way: the army fills canteens no more than two-thirds full in extreme cold (TC 21-3). Keep regular glass jars out of the cold (UC freezing jars).
Each evening, carry tomorrow's jugs from the cold rooms into the warm room.
Make a warm box: a cooler with a jug of hot water in the middle, bottles round it, the gaps stuffed with towels or paper, the lid shut and a blanket over it (Arctic Zone).
Fill a vacuum flask at night, with hot water if you have it, screw the lid on tight and keep it in your sleeping bag (TC 21-3).
Take a water bottle to bed, and by day carry one inside your coat, not in an outside pocket (TC 21-3).
steps.warn: A hot-water bottle burns skin that can't feel it. Wrap it, use warm not boiling water, and never put one in a baby's bed.

steps.text: Keep germ filters above freezing, in the warm room or inside your clothes (Sawyer freeze, Katadyn BeFree).
steps.warn: A filter that froze while wet may let germs through (Katadyn BeFree), and Sawyer says there is no definitive way to tell if freezing damaged one. Treat it as broken: boil or chlorinate instead (Sawyer FAQ).

steps.text: Thaw a frozen jug in the warm room with its cap loosened, never on the stove.

To chlorinate cold water, use plain unscented bleach, double the usual dose for water under 10 °C, and wait 1 to 2 hours. It should smell faintly of chlorine afterwards; if not, add 2 more drops per litre and wait 15 minutes more (HealthLinkBC 49b, CDC emergency).
Drink often and warm through the day, even when you're not thirsty, and make the morning's water the night before (TC 21-3).

notes:
## What the cold does to water
- **Containers split.** Water expands as it freezes: ice is about 9 % less dense than water (USGS density). A capped jug filled to the brim has nowhere for that to go. Regular glass jars are not tempered for freezing and break very easily, and jars with shoulders can break even with room left at the top (UC freezing jars).
- **Germ filters can fail out of sight.** A wet hollow-fibre filter that freezes can let germs through, and Sawyer says there is no definitive way to tell afterwards (Sawyer FAQ). See below.
- **Chlorine slows down.** Bleach works best in water around 20 °C (68 °F); for water colder than 10 °C (50 °F), HealthLinkBC doubles the dose and waits 1 to 2 hours (HealthLinkBC 49b).
- **People drink less.** The body loses a lot of fluid in the cold, and drinking only when thirsty doesn't keep up (TC 21-3).

## A day's water in the warm room
Get Prepared plans on about 4 L per person per day for drinking, cooking and sanitation (Get Prepared kits). Keep at least one day's worth, capped, in the room you heat. Keep the rest in the colder rooms only in containers that can take freezing, and carry tomorrow's jugs into the warm room each evening so they are liquid and less icy by morning. The water already in the house's pipes and tanks is a reserve too: see [Water in the building](#guides/reference_building_water).

## Containers that survive a freeze
- **Leave room.** Fill anything that might freeze only part-way. The army's rule for canteens in extreme cold is no more than two-thirds full, so the ice has room (TC 21-3).
- **Plastic, not glass.** Keep regular glass jars and bottles out of anywhere that can freeze (UC freezing jars).
- **Thaw slowly.** Bring a frozen jug into the warm room and loosen its cap. Never stand a plastic jug or a closed container on a stove: plastic softens and melts. To heat water, pour it into a pot first: see [Cooking on a wood stove](#guides/skill_cook_on_wood_stove).
- **Food-grade only,** and clean: see [Fix and clean water containers](#guides/repair_water_container) and [Food safety: storing water](#ref/reference_food_safety/storing_water).

## A cooler is a warm box too
A cooler slows heat moving either way. Arctic Zone, a cooler maker, keeps food warm in one by packing hot-water bottles around it, filling the air gaps with towels, cardboard or crumpled newspaper, keeping the lid shut, and covering the cooler with a heavy blanket (Arctic Zone). For water, put a jug of hot water in the middle, the bottles you want to keep liquid around it, stuff the gaps, close it, and throw a blanket over. Swap in a fresh hot jug when it cools. Treat it as unproven and check the bottles the first few nights: how long the warmth lasts depends on the cooler, the room and the jug.

## Flasks, coats and sleeping bags
- **Vacuum flask.** The army's one-quart steel vacuum canteen, when new, keeps water from freezing at −40 °C (−40 °F) for 6 hours. Fill it to within about 1.3 cm (½ in) of the neck and keep it in your sleeping bag at night (TC 21-3).
- **Inside your clothes by day.** Plastic canteens freeze very quickly in an outside carrier and there is no quick way to thaw them; carry one in an inside pocket, or wrapped in clothing against your back (TC 21-3).
- **In the sleeping bag at night.** A bottle of warm water warms the bag too. Hot-water bottles burn skin that can't feel them and don't belong in a baby's bed: follow [Get through winter in one heated room](#guides/skill_staying_warm).
- **Upside down.** Backcountry skiers advise storing a bottle upside down and tightly closed: freezing starts at the surface of the water, so the ice forms at the base end and the opening stays clear to drink from (Five Winds). It is a club tip, not a tested method: it buys time, it doesn't stop freezing.

## Germ filters and the cold
Hollow-fibre filters, the kind in Sawyer's filters and the Katadyn BeFree, are the ones these makers warn about. Sawyer says filters like its own must not be frozen while wet and should be kept above freezing, because ice crystals can damage the membrane (Sawyer freeze). Katadyn's BeFree manual says not to use it in freezing conditions, because a frozen membrane could let germs through and make you ill (Katadyn BeFree). Sawyer says there is no definitive way to tell if freezing damaged a filter after it was first wetted, and recommends replacing any filter that may have frozen (Sawyer FAQ). Katadyn gives a blow-through field test for a BeFree you suspect is damaged (Katadyn BeFree), but a filter that may have frozen is best treated as broken.

- Keep the filter where your water is: in the warm room, inside your coat by day and in your sleeping bag at night.
- If it may have frozen, treat it as broken and boil or chlorinate instead (Sawyer FAQ). For checking a filter that hasn't frozen, see [Test a water filter](#guides/test_water_filter).
- Even a sound one has limits: portable filters don't remove viruses (CDC emergency), and the BeFree manual says it removes neither viruses nor chemicals (Katadyn BeFree). Jug filters such as Brita are not made to remove germs from an unsafe water supply (HealthLinkBC 49b). Filter, then disinfect.

## Chlorine in cold water
Plain household bleach only: not scented, colour-safe, with added cleaners, or non-chlorine bleach (HealthLinkBC 49b). Never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or other acids, or other cleaners: it gives off toxic gas (Health Canada chemicals). See [Chemicals reference](#guides/reference_chemicals).

| Bleach on the label | Clear water above 10 °C | Cloudy, or colder than 10 °C |
|---|---|---|
| 5–9 % | 2 drops (0.1 mL) per litre, wait 30 minutes (CDC emergency) | 4 drops per litre, wait 1 to 2 hours (CDC emergency, HealthLinkBC 49b) |
| 1 % | 10 drops (0.5 mL) per litre, wait 30 minutes (CDC emergency) | 20 drops per litre, wait 1 to 2 hours (CDC emergency, HealthLinkBC 49b) |

- Most winter water is under 10 °C: snowmelt, lake water, and jugs from a cold room. Warming it toward 20 °C helps the bleach work (HealthLinkBC 49b). After the wait, the water should smell faintly of chlorine; if it doesn't, add 2 more drops per litre and wait another 15 minutes (HealthLinkBC 49b).
- Chlorine does not reliably kill Cryptosporidium (CDC Yellow Book). Boiling does: a rolling boil for 1 minute, or 2 minutes above 2,000 m (HealthLinkBC 49b).
- Old bleach loses strength: [Test bleach strength](#guides/test_bleach_strength). More on what each method stops: [Water filters: what they remove](#guides/reference_water_filters).

## Drink enough
TC 21-3 asks for at least 3.5 US quarts (about 3.3 L) a day during heavy work, as much of it hot as possible, and for the next morning's water to be made the night before (TC 21-3). Warm drinks are easier to get down in a cold house than icy ones. For making water from snow and ice, see [Water from snow and ice](#guides/skill_water_from_snow).
